scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Canadian stepdance has European origins including France, Ireland, and Scotland.

Large numbers of Scottish Gaelic settlers arrived on Cape Breton Island in Nova Scotia during the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries, bringing stepdance traditions from the Scottish Highlands and Western Islands.
While the tradition died out in Scotland, it was preserved in Canada and eventually re-introduced to its homeland.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Stepdancing served as informal domestic recreation and social leisure after hard work in lumber camps and rural villages.
Transmission was traditionally generational within the home among family and neighbours, though formal classes emerged around the 1970s.
Today it is a living tradition.
on_screen: Footage — MISSING (use images)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Canadian stepdance is normally danced in a small space with limited lateral movement.
Percussive sounds are created through a combination of foot movements such as heel taps, toe taps, and shuffles designed to accentuate the music.
Upper-body postures are typically relaxed but upright, allowing occasional arm movements that flow with the rhythm or hands on hips.
Watch for Ottawa Valley aggressive step.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Canadian stepdancing involves percussive dancing to Celtic tunes, usually played by a fiddle.
The steps strictly mirror tune types including reels, jigs, strathspeys, clogs, hornpipes, two-steps, and polkas.
Listen for the Fiddle.
The pulse is 4/4 or 6/8 at about 122 beats a minute.
Bright, melodic Celtic fiddle music driving acoustic percussive foot taps and shuffles.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Regional styles include Cape Breton stepdance in Nova Scotia, French Canadian or Quebecois stepdance taking influence from Irish and Breton dance, Ottawa Valley stepdance featuring tap elements and high aggressive steps, Newfoundland stepdance, and Métis stepdance style known as jigging.

Evolved from 18th-century Scottish Highland solo step dances, Irish step dance, Breton dance, and French traditional folk dances, with Ottawa Valley style incorporating elements of American tap dance.
